entries.c084b2150891b95db261536c413173c27945adf9: <div sID="gen14911" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Eccl.4" sID="Eccl.4"/> <div eID="gen14911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14912" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14913" type="x-p"/> Solomon, having shown the vanity of this world in the temptation which those in power feel to oppress and trample upon their subjects, here further shows, I. The temptation which the oppressed feel to discontent and impatience, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1-Eccl.4.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The temptation which those that love their case feel to take their case and neglect business, for fear of being envied, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.4-Eccl.4.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. III. The folly of hoarding up abundance of worldly wealth, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.7-Eccl.4.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>. IV. A remedy against that folly, in being made sensible of the benefit of society and mutual assistance, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.9-Eccl.4.12">ver. 9-12</reference>. V. The mutability even of royal dignity, not only through the folly of the prince himself (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.13-Eccl.4.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>), but through the fickleness of the people, let the prince be ever so discreet, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.15-Eccl.4.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>. It is not the prerogative even of kings themselves to be exempted from the vanity and vexation that attend these things; let none else then expect it.
entries.1cd267fe8b8de9b8d10bfbfe69cb589d7f96f4a1: <div eID="gen14913" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14912" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prevalence of Oppression.</title> <div sID="gen14914" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> So I returned, and considered all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold the tears of <hi type="italic">such as were</hi> oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors <hi type="italic">there was</hi> power; but they had no comforter. <hi type="super">2</hi> Wherefore I praised the dead which are already dead more than the living which are yet alive. <hi type="super">3</hi> Yea, better <hi type="italic">is he</hi> than both they, which hath not yet been, who hath not seen the evil work that is done under the sun. <div eID="gen14914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14915" type="x-p"/> Solomon had a large soul (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.29">1 Kings iv. 29</reference>) and it appeared by this, among other things, that he had a very tender concern for the miserable part of mankind and took cognizance of the afflictions of the afflicted. He had taken the oppressors to task (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16-Eccl.3.17">ch. iii. 16, 17</reference>) and put them in mind of the judgment to come, to be a curb to their insolence; now here he observes the oppressed. This he did, no doubt, as a prince, to do them justice and <hi type="italic">avenge them of their adversaries,</hi> for he both <hi type="italic">feared God and regarded men;</hi> but here he does it as a preacher, and shows, <div eID="gen14915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14916" type="x-p"/> I. The troubles of their condition (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">v. 1</reference>); of these he speaks very feelingly and with compassion. It grieved him, 1. To see might prevailing against right, to see so much <hi type="italic">oppression done under the sun,</hi> to see servants, and labourers, and poor workmen, oppressed by their masters, who take advantage of their necessity to impose what terms they please upon them, debtors oppressed by cruel creditors and creditors too by fraudulent debtors, tenants oppressed by hard landlords and orphans by treacherous guardians, and, worst of all, subjects oppressed by arbitrary princes and unjust judges. Such <hi type="italic">oppressions are done under the sun;</hi> above the sun righteousness reigns for ever. Wise men will <hi type="italic">consider these oppressions,</hi> and contrive to do something for the relief of those that are oppressed. <hi type="italic">Blessed is he that considers the poor.</hi> 2. To see how those that were wronged laid to heart the wrongs that were done them. He <hi type="italic">beheld the tears of such as were oppressed,</hi> and perhaps could not forbear weeping with them. The world is a place of weepers; look which way we will, we have a melancholy scene presented to us, <hi type="italic">the tears of</hi> those that are <hi type="italic">oppressed</hi> with one trouble or other. They find it is to no purpose to complain, and therefore mourn in secret (as Job, <reference osisRef="Job.16.20">ch. xvi. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.28">xxx. 28</reference>); but <hi type="italic">Blessed are those that mourn.</hi> 3. To see how unable they were to help themselves: <hi type="italic">On the side of their oppressors there was power,</hi> when they had done wrong, to stand to it and make good what they had done, so that the poor were borne down with a strong hand and had no way to obtain redress. It is sad to see power misplaced, and that which was given men to enable them to do good perverted to support them in doing wrong. 4. To see how they and their calamities were slighted by all about them. They wept and needed comfort, but there was none to do that friendly office: <hi type="italic">They had no comforter;</hi> their oppressors were powerful and threatening, and therefore <hi type="italic">they had no comforter;</hi> those that should have comforted them durst not, for fear of displeasing the oppressors and being made their companions for offering to be their comforters. It is sad to see so little humanity among men. <div eID="gen14916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14917" type="x-p"/> II. The temptations of their condition. Being thus hardly used, they are tempted to hate and despise life, and to envy those that are dead and in their graves, and to wish they had never been born (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.2-Eccl.4.3">v. 2, 3</reference>); and Solomon is ready to agree with them, for it serves to prove that <hi type="italic">all is vanity and vexation,</hi> since life itself is often so; and if we disregard it, in comparison with the favour and fruition of God (as St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.24">Acts xx. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.23">Phil. i. 23</reference>), it is our praise, but, if (as here) only for the sake of the miseries that attend it, it is our infirmity, and we judge therein after the flesh, as Job and Elijah did. 1. He here thinks those happy who have ended this miserable life, have done their part and quitted the stage; "<hi type="italic">I praised the dead that are already dead,</hi> slain outright, or that had a speedy passage through the world, made a short cut over the ocean of life, dead already, before they had well begun to live; I was pleased with their lot, and, had it been in their own choice, should have praised their wisdom for but looking into the world and then retiring, as not liking it. I concluded that it is better with them than with <hi type="italic">the living that are yet alive</hi> and that is all, dragging the long and heavy chain of life, and wearing out its tedious minutes." This may be compared not with <reference osisRef="Job.3.20-Job.3.21">Job iii. 20, 21</reference>, but with <reference osisRef="Rev.14.13">Rev. xiv. 13</reference>, where, in times of persecution (and such Solomon is here describing), it is not the passion of man, but the Spirit of God, that says, <hi type="italic">Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth.</hi> Note, The condition of the saints that are dead, and gone to rest with God, is upon many accounts better and more desirable than the condition of living saints that are yet continued in their work and warfare. 2. He thinks those happy who never began this miserable life; nay, they are happiest of all: <hi type="italic">He that has not been is happier than both they.</hi> Better never to have been born than be born to <hi type="italic">see the evil work that is done under the sun,</hi> to see so much wickedness committed, so much wrong done, and not only to be in no capacity to mend the matter, but to suffer ill for doing well. A good man, how calamitous a condition soever he is in in this world, cannot have cause to wish he had never been born, since he is glorifying the Lord even in the fires, and will be happy at last, for ever happy. Nor ought any to wish so while they are alive, for while there is life there is hope; a man is never undone till he is in hell.
entries.4fe0d521f2b15ea28da7872e4b4944da5eecf576: <div eID="gen14917" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prevalence of Oppression.</title> <div sID="gen14918" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Again, I considered all travail, and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour. This <hi type="italic">is</hi> also vanity and vexation of spirit. <hi type="super">5</hi> The fool foldeth his hands together, and eateth his own flesh. <hi type="super">6</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> a handful <hi type="italic">with</hi> quietness, than both the hands full <hi type="italic">with</hi> travail and vexation of spirit. <div eID="gen14918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14919" type="x-p"/> Here Solomon returns to the observation and consideration of the vanity and vexation of spirit that attend the business of this world, which he had spoken of before, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.11">ch. ii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen14919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14920" type="x-p"/> I. If a man be acute, and dexterous, and successful in his business, he gets the ill-will of <hi type="italic">his neighbours,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.4">v. 4</reference>. Though he takes a great deal of pains, and goes through <hi type="italic">all travail,</hi> does not get his estate easily, but it costs him a great deal of hard labour, nor does he get it dishonestly, he wrongs no man, defrauds no man, but by <hi type="italic">every right work,</hi> by applying himself to his own proper business, and managing it by all the rules of equity and fair dealing, yet <hi type="italic">for this he is envied of his neighbour,</hi> and the more for the reputation he has got by his honesty. This shows, 1. What little conscience most men have, that they will bear a grudge to a neighbour, give him an ill word and do him an ill turn, only because he is more ingenious and industrious than themselves, and has more of the blessing of heaven. Cain envied Abel, Esau Jacob, and Saul David, and all for their right works. This is downright diabolism. 2. What little comfort wise and useful men must expect to have in this world. Let them behave themselves ever so cautiously, they cannot escape being envied; and <hi type="italic">who can stand before envy?</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.27.4">Prov. xxvii. 4</reference>. Those that excel in virtue will always be an eye-sore to those that exceed in vice, which should not discourage us from any right work, but drive us to expect the praise of it, not from men, but from God, and not to count upon satisfaction and happiness in the creature; for, if <hi type="italic">right works</hi> prove <hi type="italic">vanity and vexation of spirit,</hi> no works <hi type="italic">under the sun</hi> can prove otherwise. But for <hi type="italic">every right work</hi> a man shall be accepted of his God, and then he needs not mind though he be <hi type="italic">envied of his neighbour,</hi> only it may make him love the world the less. <div eID="gen14920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14921" type="x-p"/> II. If a man be stupid, and dull, and blundering in his business, he does ill for himself (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The fool</hi> that goes about his work as if <hi type="italic">his hands</hi> were muffled and <hi type="italic">folded together,</hi> that does every thing awkwardly, <hi type="italic">the sluggard</hi> (for he is a fool) that loves his ease and <hi type="italic">folds his hands together</hi> to keep them warm, because they refuse to labour, he <hi type="italic">eats his own flesh,</hi> is a cannibal to himself, brings himself into such a poor condition that he has nothing to eat but his own flesh, into such a desperate condition that he is ready to eat his own flesh for vexation. He has a dog's life—hunger and ease. Because he sees active men that thrive in the world envied, he runs into the other extreme; and, lest he should be envied for his right works, he does every thing wrong, and does not deserve to be pitied. Note, Idleness is a sin that is its own punishment. The following words (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Better is a handful with quietness than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit,</hi> may be taken either, 1. As the sluggard's argument for the excuse of himself in his idleness. He <hi type="italic">folds his hands together,</hi> and abuses and misapplies a good truth for his justification, as if, because <hi type="italic">a little with quietness is better than</hi> abundance with strife, therefore a little with idleness is better than abundance with honest labour: thus <hi type="italic">wise in his own conceit</hi> is he, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.16">Prov. xxvi. 16</reference>. But, 2. I rather take it as Solomon's advice to keep the mean between that <hi type="italic">travail</hi> which will make <hi type="italic">a man envied</hi> and that slothfulness which will make a man <hi type="italic">eat his own flesh.</hi> Let us by honest industry lay hold on the handful, that we may not want necessaries, but not grasp at both the hands full, which will but create us vexation of spirit. Moderate pains and moderate gains will do best. A man may have but a handful of the world, and yet may enjoy it and himself with a great deal of <hi type="italic">quietness,</hi> with content of mind, peace of conscience, and the love and good-will of his neighbours, while many that have both their hands full, have more than heart could wish, have a great deal of travail and vexation with it. Those that cannot live on a little, it is to be feared, would not live as they should if they had ever so much.
entries.3dd0984cb6195e3810c1dc5c7786743ad709887a: <div eID="gen14921" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vanity of Human Wishes.</title> <div sID="gen14922" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Then I returned, and I saw vanity under the sun. <hi type="super">8</hi> There is one <hi type="italic">alone,</hi> and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> not a second; yea, he hath neither child nor brother: yet <hi type="italic">is there</hi> no end of all his labour; neither is his eye satisfied with riches; neither <hi type="italic">saith he,</hi> For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good? This <hi type="italic">is</hi> also vanity, yea, it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a sore travail. <hi type="super">9</hi> Two <hi type="italic">are</hi> better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. <hi type="super">10</hi> For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him <hi type="italic">that is</hi> alone when he falleth; for <hi type="italic">he hath</hi> not another to help him up. <hi type="super">11</hi> Again, if two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm <hi type="italic">alone?</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken. <div eID="gen14922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14923" type="x-p"/> Here Solomon fastens upon another instance of the vanity of this world, that frequently the more men have of it the more they would have; and on this they are so intent that they have no enjoyment of what they have. Now Solomon here shows, <div eID="gen14923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14924" type="x-p"/> I. That selfishness is the cause of this evil (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.7-Eccl.4.8">v. 7, 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is one alone,</hi> that minds none but himself, cares for nobody, but would, if he could, be placed alone in the midst of the earth; <hi type="italic">there is not a second,</hi> nor does he desire there should be: one mouth he thinks enough in a house, and grudges every thing that goes beside him. See how this covetous muckworm is here described. 1. He makes himself a mere slave to his business. Though <hi type="italic">he has</hi> no charge, <hi type="italic">neither child nor brother,</hi> none to take care of but himself, none to hang upon him, or draw from him, no poor relations, nor dares he marry, for fear of the expense of a family, <hi type="italic">yet is there no end of his labour;</hi> he is at it night and day, early and late, and will scarcely allow necessary rest to himself and those he employs. He does not confine himself within the bounds of his own calling, but is for having a hand in any thing that he can get by. See <reference osisRef="Ps.127.2">Ps. cxxvii. 2</reference>. 2. He never thinks he has enough: <hi type="italic">His eye is not satisfied with riches.</hi> Covetousness is called <hi type="italic">the lust of the eye</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.2.16">1 John ii. 16</reference>) because the <hi type="italic">beholding of it with his eyes</hi> is all that the worldling seems to covet, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">Eccl. v. 11</reference>. He has enough for his back (as bishop Reynolds observes), for his belly, for his calling, for his family, for his living decently in the world, but he has not enough for his eyes. Though he can but see it, can but count his money, and not find in his heart to use it, yet he is not easy because he has not more to regale his eyes with. 3. He denies himself the comfort of what he has: he <hi type="italic">bereaves his soul of good.</hi> If our souls are bereaved of good, it is we ourselves that do bereave them. Others may bereave us of outward good, but cannot rob us of our graces and comforts, our spiritual good things. It is our own fault if we do not enjoy ourselves. Yet many are so set upon the world that, in pursuit of it, they <hi type="italic">bereave their souls of good</hi> here and for ever, make shipwreck of faith and of a good conscience, bereave themselves not only of the favour of God and eternal life, but of the pleasures of this world too and this present life. Worldly people, pretending to be wise for themselves, are really enemies to themselves. 4. He has no excuse for doing this: <hi type="italic">He has neither child nor brother,</hi> none that he is bound to, on whom he may lay out what he has to his satisfaction while he lives, none that he has a kindness for, for whom he may lay it up to his satisfaction and to whom he may leave it when he dies, none that are poor or dear to him. 5. He has not consideration enough to show himself the folly of this. He never puts this question to himself, "<hi type="italic">For whom do I labour</hi> thus? Do I labour, as I should, for the glory of God, and that I may have to give to those that need? Do I consider that it is but for the body that I am labouring, a dying body; it is for others, and I know not for whom—perhaps for a fool, that will scatter it as fast as I have gathered it—perhaps for a foe, that will be ungrateful to my memory?" Note, It is wisdom for those that take pains about this world to consider whom they take all this pains for, and whether it be really worth while to bereave themselves of good that they may bestow it on a stranger. If men do not consider this, it <hi type="italic">is vanity, and a sore travail;</hi> they shame and vex themselves to no purpose. <div eID="gen14924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14925" type="x-p"/> II. That sociableness is the cure of this evil. Men are thus sordid because they are all for themselves. Now Solomon shows here, by divers instances, that <hi type="italic">it is not good for man to be alone</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.18">Gen. ii. 18</reference>); he designs hereby to recommend to us both marriage and friendship, two things which covetous misers decline, because of the charge of them; but such are the comfort and advantage of them both, if prudently contracted, that they will very well quit cost. Man, in paradise itself, could not be happy without a mate, and therefore is no sooner made than matched. 1. Solomon lays this down for a truth, That <hi type="italic">two are better than one,</hi> and more happy jointly than either of them could be separately, more pleased in one another than they could be in themselves only, mutually serviceable to each other's welfare, and by a united strength more likely to do good to others: <hi type="italic">They have a good reward of their labour;</hi> whatever service they do, it is returned to them another way. He that serves himself only has himself only for his paymaster, and commonly proves more unjust and ungrateful to himself than his friend, if he should serve him, would be to him; witness him that <hi type="italic">labours endlessly</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">bereaves his soul of good;</hi> he has no <hi type="italic">reward of his labour.</hi> But he that is kind to another has <hi type="italic">a good reward;</hi> the pleasure and advantage of holy love will be an abundant recompence for all the <hi type="italic">work and labour of love.</hi> Hence Solomon infers the mischief of solitude: <hi type="italic">Woe to him that is alone.</hi> He lies exposed to many temptations which good company and friendship would prevent and help him to guard against; he wants that advantage which a man has by the countenance of his friend, as iron has of being sharpened by iron. A monastic life then was surely never intended for a state of perfection, nor should those be reckoned the greatest lovers of God who cannot find in their hearts to love any one else. 2. He proves it by divers instances of the benefit of friendship and good conversation. (1.) Occasional succour in an exigency. It is good for two to travel together, <hi type="italic">for if</hi> one happen to <hi type="italic">fall,</hi> he may be lost for want of a little help. If a man fall <hi type="italic">into sin,</hi> his friend will help to <hi type="italic">restore him with the spirit of meekness;</hi> if he fall into trouble, his friend will help to comfort him and assuage his grief. (2.) Mutual warmth. As a fellow-traveller is of use (<hi type="italic">amicus pro vehiculo</hi>—<hi type="italic">a friend is a good substitute for a carriage</hi>) so is a bedfellow: <hi type="italic">If two lie together, they have heat.</hi> So virtuous and gracious affections are excited by good society, and Christians warm one another by <hi type="italic">provoking one another to love and to good works.</hi> (3.) United strength. If an enemy find a man alone, he is likely to <hi type="italic">prevail against him;</hi> with his own single strength he cannot make his part good, but, if he have a second, he may do well enough: <hi type="italic">two shall withstand him.</hi> "You shall help me against my enemy, and I will help you against yours;" according to the agreement between Joab and Abishai (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.11">2 Sam. x. 11</reference>), and so both are conquerors; whereas, acting separately, both would have been conquered; as was said of the ancient Britons, when the Romans invaded them, <hi type="italic">Dum singuli pugnant, universi vincuntur—While they fight in detached parties, they sacrifice the general cause.</hi> In our spiritual warfare we may be helpful to one another as well as in our spiritual work; next to the comfort of communion with God, is that of the communion of saints. He concludes with this proverb, <hi type="italic">A threefold cord is not easily broken,</hi> any more than a bundle of arrows, though each single thread, and each single arrow, is. Two together he compares to <hi type="italic">a threefold cord;</hi> for where two are closely joined in holy love and fellowship, Christ will by his Spirit come to them, and make the third, as he joined himself to the two disciples going to Emmaus, and then there is <hi type="italic">a threefold cord</hi> that can never be <hi type="italic">broken. They that dwell in love, dwell in God, and God in them.</hi>
entries.8f93aa6b952d026df3ffa3ae24ba0aa46898d78e: <div eID="gen14925" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Advantages of Society.</title> <div sID="gen14926" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished. <hi type="super">14</hi> For out of prison he cometh to reign; whereas also <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> born in his kingdom becometh poor. <hi type="super">15</hi> I considered all the living which walk under the sun, with the second child that shall stand up in his stead. <hi type="super">16</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> no end of all the people, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of all that have been before them: they also that come after shall not rejoice in him. Surely this also <hi type="italic">is</hi> vanity and vexation of spirit. <div eID="gen14926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14927" type="x-p"/> Solomon was himself a king, and therefore may be allowed to speak more freely than another concerning the vanity of kingly state and dignity, which he shows here to be an uncertain thing; he had before said so (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.24">Prov. xxvii. 24</reference>, <hi type="italic">The crown doth not endure to every generation</hi>), and his son found it so. Nothing is more slippery than the highest post of honour without wisdom and the people's love. <div eID="gen14927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14928" type="x-p"/> I. A king is not happy unless he have wisdom, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.13-Eccl.4.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. He that is truly <hi type="italic">wise,</hi> prudent, and pious, though he be <hi type="italic">poor</hi> in the world, and very young, and upon both accounts despised and little taken notice of, <hi type="italic">is better,</hi> more truly valuable and worthy of respect, is likely to do better for himself and to be a greater blessing to his generation, <hi type="italic">than a king, than an old king,</hi> and therefore venerable both for his gravity and for his dignity, if he be <hi type="italic">foolish,</hi> and knows not how to manage public affairs himself nor <hi type="italic">will be admonished</hi> and advised by others—<hi type="italic">who</hi> knows not to <hi type="italic">be admonished,</hi> that is, will not suffer any counsel or admonition to be given him (no one about him dares contradict him) or will not hearken to the counsel and admonition that are given him. It is so far from being any part of the honour of kings that it is the greatest dishonour to them that can be not to be <hi type="italic">admonished.</hi> Folly and wilfulness commonly go together, and those that most need admonition can worst bear it; but neither age nor titles will secure men respect if they have not true wisdom and virtue to recommend them; while wisdom and virtue will gain men honour even under the disadvantages of youth and poverty. To prove the <hi type="italic">wise child better than the foolish king</hi> he shows what each of them comes to, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.14">v. 14</reference>. 1. <hi type="italic">A poor</hi> man by his wisdom comes to be preferred, as Joseph, who, when he was but young, was brought <hi type="italic">out of prison</hi> to be <hi type="italic">the second</hi> man in the kingdom, to which story Solomon seems here to refer. Providence sometimes <hi type="italic">raises the poor out of the dust, to set them among princes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.113.7-Ps.113.8">Ps. cxiii. 7, 8</reference>. Wisdom has wrought not only the liberty of men, but their dignity, raised them from the dunghill, from the dungeon, to the throne. 2. <hi type="italic">A king</hi> by his folly and wilfulness comes to be impoverished. Though he was <hi type="italic">born in his kingdom,</hi> came to it by inheritance, though he has lived to be old in it and has had time to fill his treasures, yet if he take ill courses, and <hi type="italic">will no more be admonished</hi> as he has been, thinking, because he is old, he is past it, he <hi type="italic">becomes poor;</hi> his treasure is exhausted, and perhaps he is forced to resign his crown and retire into privacy. <div eID="gen14928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14929" type="x-p"/> II. A king is not likely to continue if he have not a confirmed interest in the affections of the people; this is intimated, but somewhat obscurely, in the last <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.15-Eccl.4.16">two verses</reference>. 1. He that is king must have a successor, a <hi type="italic">second,</hi> a <hi type="italic">child that shall stand up in his stead,</hi> his own, suppose, or perhaps that <hi type="italic">poor and wise child</hi> spoken of, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.12">v. 13</reference>. Kings, when they grow old, must have the mortification of seeing those that are to jostle them out and stand up in their stead. 2. It is common with the people to adore the rising sun: <hi type="italic">All the living who walk under the sun</hi> are <hi type="italic">with the second child,</hi> are in his interests, are conversant with him, and make their court to him more than to the father, whom they look upon as going off, and despise because his best days are past. Solomon considered this; he saw this to be the disposition of his own people, which appeared immediately after his death, in their complaints of his government and their affectation of a change. 3. People are never long easy and satisfied: <hi type="italic">There is no end,</hi> no rest, <hi type="italic">of all the people;</hi> they are continually fond of changes, and know not what they would have. 4. This is no new thing, but it has been the way <hi type="italic">of all that have been before them;</hi> there have been instances of this in every age: even Samuel and David could not always please. 5. As it has been, so it is likely to be still: <hi type="italic">Those that come after</hi> will be of the same spirit, and <hi type="italic">shall not</hi> long <hi type="italic">rejoice in him</hi> whom at first they seemed extremely fond of. To-day, <hi type="italic">Hosanna</hi>—tomorrow, <hi type="italic">Crucify.</hi> 6. It cannot but be a great grief to princes to see themselves thus slighted by those they have studied to oblige and have depended upon; there is no faith in man, no stedfastness. <hi type="italic">This is vanity and vexation of spirit.</hi>  <chapter eID="Eccl.4"/> <div eID="gen14929" type="x-p"/>

entries.943c255a305d122ef4b0af03b6c5cd24860c55b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8041"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen12486" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1-Eccl.4.16">Ec 4:1-16</reference>.<div eID="gen12486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12487" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8041"/><hi type="bold">1. returned--</hi>namely, to the thought set forth (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ec 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.35.9">Job 35:9</reference>).<div eID="gen12487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">power--</hi>Maurer, not so well, "violence."<div eID="gen12488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no comforter--</hi>twice said to express continued suffering without any to give comfort (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.7">Is 53:7</reference>). <div eID="gen12489" type="x-p"/>
entries.a29ad9e13e58fe3efc2bdf930e710d929af7f4a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8042"/><div sID="gen12490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8042"/>2. A profane sentiment if severed from its connection; but just in its bearing on Solomon's scope. If religion were not taken into account (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">Ec 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.19">19</reference>), to die as soon as possible would be desirable, so as not to suffer or witness "oppressions"; and still more so, not to be born at all (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Ec 7:1</reference>). Job (<reference osisRef="Job.3.12">Job 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.7">21:7</reference>), David (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.3">Psa 73:3</reference>, &c.), Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jr 12:1</reference>), Habakkuk (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Ha 1:13</reference>), all passed through the same perplexity, until they went into the sanctuary, and looked beyond the present to the "judgment" (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">Psa 73:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.20">Ha 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.17">3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">18</reference>). Then they saw the need of delay, before completely punishing the wicked, to give space for repentance, or else for accumulation of wrath (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.15">Ro 2:15</reference>); and before completely rewarding the godly, to give room for faith and perseverance in tribulation (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.7-Ps.92.12">Psa 92:7-12</reference>). Earnests, however, are often even now given, by partial judgments of the future, to assure us, in spite of difficulties, that God governs the earth. <div eID="gen12490" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2f801f34d51236774c5ae376d6babb5fe72e34e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8043"/><div sID="gen12491" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8043"/><hi type="bold">3. not seen--</hi>nor experienced. <div eID="gen12491" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc58f0f145879800ef38d753f990a38ebaea1c2c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8044"/><div sID="gen12492" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8044"/><hi type="bold">4. right--</hi>rather, "prosperous" (see on <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.21">Ec 2:21</reference>). Prosperity, which men so much covet, is the very source of provoking oppression (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Ec 4:1</reference>) and "envy," so far is it from constituting the chief good. <div eID="gen12492" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f4203d5dd1f8b39b7521bc20f445e80a4133b09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8045"/><div sID="gen12493" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8045"/>5. Still the<div eID="gen12493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12494" type="x-p"/> fool (the wicked oppressor) is not to be envied even in this life, who "folds his hands together" in idleness (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.10">Pr 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.33">24:33</reference>), living on the means he wrongfully wrests from others; for such a one<div eID="gen12494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12495" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eateth his own flesh--</hi>that is, is a self-tormentor, never satisfied, his spirit preying on itself (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.20">Is 9:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.26">49:26</reference>). <div eID="gen12495" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae729f095c0e826e8c85c721c1379ff0d078feae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8046"/><div sID="gen12496" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8046"/>6. Hebrew; "One open hand (palm) full of quietness, than both closed hands full of travail." "Quietness" (mental tranquillity flowing from honest labor), opposed to "eating one's own flesh" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.5">Ec 4:5</reference>), also opposed to anxious labor to gain (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.8">Ec 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.15.16">Pr 15:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.8">16:8</reference>). <div eID="gen12496" type="x-p"/>
entries.01a57f92633a0189adeaf2c1978c15e65aa067dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8047"/><div sID="gen12497" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8047"/>7. A vanity described in <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.8">Ec 4:8</reference>. <div eID="gen12497" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e84d6467d5f2d9f7909344fa190cfc6015b9c69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8048"/><div sID="gen12498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8048"/><hi type="bold">8. not a second--</hi>no partner.<div eID="gen12498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">child--</hi>"son or brother," put for any heir (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.5-Deut.25.10">De 25:5-10</reference>).<div eID="gen12499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eye--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.8">Ec 1:8</reference>). The miser would not be able to give an account of his infatuation. <div eID="gen12500" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8fed448f170a59f61b528e5f0dcad96800c7dc4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8049"/><div sID="gen12501" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8049"/><hi type="bold">9. Two--</hi>opposed to "one" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.8">Ec 4:8</reference>). Ties of union, marriage, friendship, religious communion, are better than the selfish solitariness of the miser (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.18">Ge 2:18</reference>).<div eID="gen12501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reward--</hi>Advantage accrues from their efforts being conjoined. The Talmud says, "A man without a companion is like a left hand without the right. <div eID="gen12502" type="x-p"/>
entries.77d5e33336f1128c29958f18580e4754c73ed0dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8050"/><div sID="gen12503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8050"/><hi type="bold">10. if they fall--</hi>if the one or other fall, as may happen to both, namely, into any distress of body, mind, or soul. <div eID="gen12503" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee88602bf1c7549d41a90bd73c0ac79e1ef58a0c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8051"/><div sID="gen12504" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8051"/>11. (See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.1">1Ki 1:1</reference>). The image is taken from man and wife, but applies universally to the warm sympathy derived from social ties. So Christian ties (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.32">Lu 24:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.28.15">Ac 28:15</reference>). <div eID="gen12504" type="x-p"/>
entries.91f805fdca559c9a9a7c218bbd9419f8e09cd110: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8052"/><div sID="gen12505" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8052"/><hi type="bold">12. one--</hi>enemy.<div eID="gen12505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12506" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">threefold cord--</hi>proverbial for a combination of many--for example, husband, wife, and children (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.14">Pr 11:14</reference>); so Christians (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.1">Lu 10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>, 19). Untwist the cord, and the separate threads are easily "broken." <div eID="gen12506" type="x-p"/>
entries.2265a3066ec1705eb7d23178dc460e809e7daac5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8053"/><div sID="gen12507" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8053"/>13. The "threefold cord" [Ec 4:12] of social ties suggests the subject of civil government. In this case too, he concludes that kingly power confers no lasting happiness. The "wise" child, though a supposed case of Solomon, answers, in the event foreseen by the Holy Ghost, to Jeroboam, then a poor but valiant youth, once a "servant" of Solomon, and (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.26-1Kgs.11.40">1Ki 11:26-40</reference>) appointed by God through the prophet Ahijah to be heir of the kingdom of the ten tribes about to be rent from Rehoboam. The "old and foolish king" answers to Solomon himself, who had lost his wisdom, when, in defiance of two warnings of God (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.14">1Ki 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.2-1Kgs.9.9">9:2-9</reference>), he forsook God.<div eID="gen12507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will no more be admonished--</hi>knows not yet how to take warning (see Margin) God had by Ahijah already intimated the judgment coming on Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.11-1Kgs.11.13">1Ki 11:11-13</reference>). <div eID="gen12508" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8043ee357f12e8418394972b1d4e01a7c803b37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8054"/><div sID="gen12509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8054"/><hi type="bold">14. out of prison--</hi>Solomon uses this phrase of a supposed case; for example, Joseph raised from a dungeon to be lord of Egypt. His words are at the same time so framed by the Holy Ghost that they answer virtually to Jeroboam, who fled to escape a "prison" and death from Solomon, to Shishak of Egypt (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.40">1Ki 11:40</reference>). This unconscious presaging of his own doom, and that of Rehoboam, constitutes the irony. David's elevation from poverty and exile, under Saul (which may have been before Solomon's mind), had so far their counterpart in that of Jeroboam.<div eID="gen12509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whereas ... becometh poor--</hi>rather, "though he (the youth) was born poor in his kingdom" (in the land where afterwards he was to reign). <div eID="gen12510" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfb6c17b6ede4ed420a5b0a35f09b8bb7b10ab07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8055"/><div sID="gen12511" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8055"/>15. "I considered all the living," the present generation, in relation to ("with") the "second youth" (the "legitimate successor" of the "old king," as opposed to the "poor youth," the one first spoken of, about to be raised from poverty to a throne), that is, Rehoboam.<div eID="gen12511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in his stead--</hi>the old king's. <div eID="gen12512" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a3a07f89ed2acba9fbec11b199f2b65350f0261: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8056"/><div sID="gen12513" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8056"/>16. Notwithstanding their now worshipping the rising sun, the heir-apparent, I reflected that "there were no bounds, no stability (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.6">2Sa 15:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.1">20:1</reference>), no check on the love of innovation, of all that have been before them," that is, the past generation; so<div eID="gen12513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also they that come after--</hi>that is, the next generation,<div eID="gen12514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall not rejoice in him--</hi>namely, Rehoboam. The parallel, "shall not rejoice," fixes the sense of "no bounds," no permanent adherence, though now men rejoice in him. <chapter eID="Eccl.4"/>

entries.9bab08c092158c6bc945752bf879336034a08b23: <div eID="gen25412" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen25413" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25414" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25414" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25413" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25415" type="x-p"/> The vanity of life is increased by oppression, <reference osisRef="Ecc.4.1-Ecc.4.3">Ecc 4:1-3</reference>; by envy, <reference osisRef="Ecc.4.4">Ecc 4:4</reference>; by idleness, <reference osisRef="Ecc.4.5">Ecc 4:5</reference>. The misery of a solitary life, and the advantages of society, <reference osisRef="Ecc.4.6-Ecc.4.12">Ecc 4:6-12</reference>. A poor and wise child; better than an old and foolish king, <reference osisRef="Ecc.4.13">Ecc 4:13</reference>. The uncertainty of popular favor, <reference osisRef="Ecc.4.14-Ecc.4.16">Ecc 4:14-16</reference>. <div eID="gen25415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25416" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen25416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25417" type="x-p"/> Considered all the oppressions - עשקים ashukim signifies any kind of injury which a man can receive in his person, his property, or his good fame. <div eID="gen25417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25418" type="x-p"/> On the side of their oppressors there was power - And, therefore, neither protection nor comfort for the oppressed.
entries.0a79479b7e9bce420a0b99b728d230bdfb5e58e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen25418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25419" type="x-p"/> Wherefore I praised the dead - I considered those happy who had escaped from the pilgrimage of life to the place where the wicked cease from troubling, and where the weary are at rest.
entries.99afcb45db6eb0dc1e21220b8ae47a67d9d3839a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen25419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25420" type="x-p"/> Which hath not yet been - Better never to have been born into the world, than to have seen and suffered so many miseries.
entries.ad596a75f4f95b402d60c638a0fa50546a7440a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen25420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25421" type="x-p"/> For this a man is envied - It is not by injustice and wrong only that men suffer, but through envy also. For if a man act uprightly and properly in the world, he soon becomes the object of his neighbor's envy and calumny too. Therefore the encouragement to do good, to act an upright part, is very little. This constitutes a part of the vain and empty system of human life.
entries.0aa3abcb744a14511c8047a497b1f5e4e9dce819: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen25421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25422" type="x-p"/> The fool foldeth his hands - After all, without labor and industry no man can get any comfort in life; and he who gives way to idleness is the veriest of fools.
entries.78806783f36174d62d11a2fb427065d6fbcb8270: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen25422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25423" type="x-p"/> Better is a handful with quietness - These may be the words of the slothful man, and spoken in vindication of his idleness; as if he had said, "Every man who labors and amasses property is the object of envy, and is marked by the oppressor as a subject for spoil; better, therefore, to act as I do; gain little, and have little, and enjoy my handful with quietness." Or the words may contain Solomon's reflection on the subject.
entries.f4bf798b69e07f57aa4182a96b3b7a8605c8b0bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen25423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25424" type="x-p"/> There is one alone, and there is not a second - Here covetousness and avarice are characterized. The man who is the center of his own existence; has neither wife, child, nor legal heir; and yet is as intent on getting money as if he had the largest family to provide for; nor does he only labor with intense application, but he even refuses himself the comforts of life out of his own gains! This is not only vanity, the excess of foolishness, but it is also sore travail.
entries.6f5a966444aee76852de24fd6ccb6e771c806340: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen25424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25425" type="x-p"/> Two are better than one - Married life is infinitely to be preferred to this kind of life, for the very reasons alleged below, and which require no explanation.
entries.1fdfaec1cb1460520daa8ba3ae9dca3c0921f25b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen25425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25426" type="x-p"/> Better is a poor and a wise child - The Targum applies this to Abraham. "Abraham was a poor child of only three years of age; but he had the spirit of prophecy, and he refused to worship the idols which the old foolish king - Nimrod - had set up; therefore Nimrod cast him into a furnace of fire. But the Lord worked a miracle and delivered him. Yet here was no knowledge in Nimrod, and he would not be admonished." The Targum proceeds:
entries.4f3aa1f4869fc7c60909b4f94ac90c75d73be5fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen25426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25427" type="x-p"/> For out of prison he cometh to reign - "Then Abraham left the country of the idolaters, where he had been imprisoned, and came and reigned over the land of Canaan; and Nimrod became poor in this world." This is the fact to which the ancient rabbins supposed Solomon to allude.
entries.7dd5f5e6fce8d88c483fd1ef89516761fc4ff73f: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen25427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25428" type="x-p"/> With the second child that shall stand up - The Targum applies this to the case of Jeroboam and Rehoboam. History affords many instances of mean persons raised to sovereign authority, and of kings being reduced to the meanest offices, and to a morsel of bread. Agrippa himself ascended the throne of Israel after having been long in prison. See Josephus, Ant. lib. 18: c. 8. This the heathens attributed to fortune. <div eID="gen25428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25429" type="x-p"/> Si fortuna volet, fies de rhetore consul; <div eID="gen25429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25430" type="x-p"/> Si volet haec eadem, fies de consule rhetor. <div eID="gen25430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25431" type="x-p"/> Juv. Sat. vii., ver. 197. <div eID="gen25431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25432" type="x-p"/> Though I have given what the Jews suppose to be the allusion in these verses, yet the reader may doubt whether the reference be correct. There is a case implied, whether from fact or assumption I cannot say; but it seems to be this: <div eID="gen25432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25433" type="x-p"/> A king who had abused the authority vested in him by oppressing the people, had a son whose prudent conduct promised much comfort to the nation, when he should come to the throne. The father, seeing the popular wish, and becoming jealous of his son, shut him up in prison. In the interim the old king either dies or is deposed, and the son is brought out of prison, and placed on the throne. Then (<reference osisRef="Ecc.4.15">Ecc 4:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.4.16">Ecc 4:16</reference>) multitudes of the people flock to him, and begin to walk under the sun; i.e., the prosperous state to which the nation is raised by its redemption from the former tyranny. However, the wise man insinuates that this sunshine will not last long. The young king, feeling the reins in his own hands, and being surrounded by those whose interest it was to flatter in order to obtain and continue in court favor, he also becomes corrupted so that those who come after shall have no cause of rejoicing in him. This appears to be the case; and similar cases have frequently occurred, not only in Asiatic, but also in European history, I have, in another place, referred to the case of Rushn Achter, who was brought out of prison and set upon the throne of Hindoostan. This is expressed in the following elegant Persian couplet, where his fortune is represented as similar to that of the patriarch Joseph: - "The bright star is now become a moon: <div eID="gen25433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25434" type="x-p"/> Joseph is taken out of prison, and become a king." <div eID="gen25434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25435" type="x-p"/> Rushn Achter signifies a bright or splendid star.
entries.a4442e592fdf7910577b20adeb92f0d7ae7aa187: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen25435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25436" type="x-p"/> There is no end of all the people - This is supposed to refer to the multitudes of people who hail the advent and accession of a new sovereign; for, as Suetonius remarks, A plerisque adorari solem orientem, "Most people adore the rising sun." But when the new king becomes old, very few regard him; and perhaps he lives long enough to be as much despised by the very persons who before were ready to worship him. This is also a miserable vanity. Thus the blooming heir: - "Shall feel the sad reverse: honored awhile; <div eID="gen25436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25437" type="x-p"/> Then, like his sire, contemn'd, abhorr'd, forgot." <div eID="gen25437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25438" type="x-p"/> C.  <chapter eID="Eccl.4"/> <div eID="gen25438" type="x-p"/>

entries.af21e73a379675cbb4d23adbe84f3c0aa631b37b: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Ecc 4:1</reference> “And again I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold there the tears of the oppressed, and they have no comforter; and from the hand of their oppressors goeth forth violence; and they have no comforter.” Incorrectly Hahn: And anew I saw, - the observation is different from that of <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ecc 3:16</reference>, though cognate. Thus: And again I saw, - the expression follows the syntactic scheme of <reference osisRef="Gen.26.18">Gen 26:18</reference>; regarding the <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. brought into view here and at Ecc 4:7. The second העשׁ is <hi type="italic">part. pass</hi>.; the first, as at <reference osisRef="Job.35.9">Job 35:9</reference>, and also at <reference osisRef="Amos.3.9">Amo 3:9</reference>, is abstract (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, bringing the many separate instances under one general idea) <hi type="italic">pluraletantum</hi> (cf. פּדוּיי, <hi type="italic">redemti</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.10">Isa 35:10</reference>; and <hi type="italic">redemtio, pretium redemtionis</hi>, Num 3:46); the plur. נע אשׁר need not appear strange, since even חיּים is connected with the plur. of the pred., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.11">Psa 31:11</reference>; Psa 88:4. דּמעת has, as at <reference osisRef="Isa.25.8">Isa 25:8</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Rev.21.4">Rev 21:4</reference>, πᾶν δάκρυον), a collective sense. The expression כּח ... וּמיּד is singular. According to the most natural impression, it seems to signify: “and from the hand of their oppressors no power of deliverance” (carrying forward אין); but the parallelism of the palindromically constructed verse (as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.6">Ecc 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.10">Ecc 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ecc 3:16</reference>) excludes this meaning. Thus כּח is here once-nowhere else-used, like the Greek βία, in the sense of violence; Luzzatto prefers the reading וּביד, by which the expression would be in conformity with the linguistic usage; but also מיד is explained: the force which they have in their hands is, in going forth from their hands, thought of as abused, and, as taking the form of שׁד or חזקה. In view of this sorrow which men bring upon their fellow-men, life for Koheleth lost all its worth and attraction.
entries.f2e1bd7bc54191d53cac77b26a526278c8646251: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.2-Eccl.4.3">Ecc 4:2-3</reference> “And I praised the dead who were long ago dead, more than the living who are yet in life; and as happier than both, him who has not yet come into existence, who hath not seen the evil work which is done under the sun.” ושׁבּח is hardly thought of as part., like יוּקשׁים = מיקּשׁים, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">Ecc 9:12</reference>; the m of the <hi type="italic">part</hi>. <hi type="italic">Pih</hi>. is not usually thrown away, only מהר, Zep 1:14, is perhaps = ממהר, but for the same reason as בּית־אל, 2Ki 2:3, is = בּבית - אל. Thus ושׁבּח, like ונתון, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.9">Ecc 8:9</reference>, is <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. <hi type="italic">absol</hi>., which is used to continue, in an adverbially subord. manner, the preceding finite with the same subject,<note placement="foot">Also <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.20">1Ch 5:20</reference>, the subject remains virtually the same: <hi type="italic">et ita quidem ut exaudirentur</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen12261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12262" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Gen.41.43">Gen 41:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.25.14">Lev 25:14</reference>; Jdg 7:19, etc.; cf. especially <reference osisRef="Exod.8.11">Exo 8:11</reference> : “Pharaoh saw ... and hardened (והכבּד) his heart;” just in the same manner as ושׁבּח here connects itself with ושׁ אני וא. Only the annexed designation of the subject is peculiar; the syntactic possibility of this connection is established by <reference osisRef="Ps.15.5">Psa 15:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.40.2">Job 40:2</reference>, and, in the second rank, by <reference osisRef="Gen.17.10">Gen 17:10</reference>; Eze 5:14. Yet אני might well enough have been omitted had וש אני וא not stood too remote. Regarding עדנה<note placement="foot">Thus punctuated with <hi type="italic">Segol</hi> under <hi type="italic">Daleth</hi>, and ,נ raphatum, in F. H. J. P. Thus also Kimchi in <hi type="italic">W.B</hi>. under עד.</note> and עדן. The circumstantial form of the expression: <hi type="italic">prae vivis qui vivi sunt adhuc</hi>, is intentional: they who are as yet living must be witnesses of the manifold and comfortless human miseries. <div eID="gen12262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12263" type="x-p"/> It is a question whether <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.3">Ecc 4:3</reference> begins a new clause (lxx, Syr., and Venet.) or not. That את, like the Arab. aiya, sometimes serves to give prominence to the subject, cannot be denied (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Böttcher, §516, and Mühlau’s remarks thereto). The Mishnic expressions היּום אותו, that day, הארץ אותהּ, that land, and the like (Geiger, §14. 2), presuppose a certain preparation in the older language; and we might, with Weiss (<hi type="italic">Stud. ueber d. Spr. der Mishna</hi>, p. 112), interpret אשׁר את in the sense of אותי אשר, <hi type="italic">is qui</hi>. But the accus. rendering is more natural. Certainly the expression טוב שׁבּח, “to praise,” “to pronounce happy,” is not used; but to טוב it is natural to suppose וקראתי added. Jerome accordingly translates: <hi type="italic">et feliciorem utroque judicavi qui necdum natus est</hi>. הרע has the double <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi>, as is generally the case, except at <reference osisRef="Ps.54.7">Psa 54:7</reference> and Mic 7:3.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Heidenheim, <hi type="italic">Meor Enajim</hi>, under Deu 17:7.</note> <div eID="gen12263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12264" type="x-p"/> Better than he who is born is the unborn, who does not become conscious of the wicked actions that are done under the sun. A similar thought, with many variations in its expression, is found in Greek writers; see regarding these shrill discordances, which run through all the joy of the beauty and splendour of Hellenic life, my <hi type="italic">Apologetick</hi>, p. 116. Buddhism accordingly gives to <hi type="italic">nirvâna</hi> the place of the highest good. That we find Koheleth on the same path (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.3">Ecc 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Ecc 7:1</reference>), has its reason in this, that so long as the central point of man’s existence lies in the present life, and this is not viewed as the fore-court of eternity, there is no enduring consolation to lift us above the miseries of this present world.
entries.92af8e3e5a86f77dbfefb5cd34b247b8dafc7f5a: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.4">Ecc 4:4</reference> “And I saw all the labour and all the skill of business, that it is an envious surpassing of the one by the other: also this is vain and windy effort.” The היא refers to this exertion of vigorous effort and skill. The Graec. Venet., by rendering here and at <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.24">Ecc 2:24</reference> כּשׁרון, by καθαρότης, betrays himself as a Jew. With כּי, <hi type="italic">quod</hi>, that which forms the pred. follows the object. the <hi type="italic">min</hi> in mere'ehu is as in <hi type="italic">amatz min</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.18">Psa 18:18</reference>, and the like - the same as the compar.: <hi type="italic">aemulatio qua unus prae altero eminere studet</hi>. All this expenditure of strength and art has covetousness and envy, with which one seeks to surpass another, as its poisoned sting.
entries.f11c51395a3806359b752578292fb22765f106c4: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.5">Ecc 4:5</reference> <div eID="gen12264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12265" type="x-p"/> There ought certainly to be activity according to our calling; indolence is self-destruction: “The fool foldeth his hands, and eateth his own flesh.” He layeth his hands together (Prov 6:10-24:33), - placeth them in his bosom, instead of using them in working, - and thereby he eateth himself up, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, bringeth ruin upon himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.2">Psa 27:2</reference>; Mic 3:3; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.26">Isa 49:26</reference>); for instead of nourishing himself by the labour of his hands, he feeds on his own flesh, and thus wasteth away. The emphasis does not lie on the subject (the fool, and only the fool), but on the pred.
entries.8ba4ed502c337f0d363b71452c916c834781d0c5: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.6">Ecc 4:6</reference> <div eID="gen12265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12266" type="x-p"/> The fifth verse stands in a relation of contrast to this which follows: “Better is one hand full of quietness, than both fists full of labour and windy effort.” Mendelssohn and others interpret <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.5">Ecc 4:5</reference> as the objection of the industrious, and <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.6">Ecc 4:6</reference> as the reply of the slothful. Zöckler agrees with Hitz., and lapses into the hypothesis of a dialogue otherwise rejected by him. As everywhere, so also here it preserves the unity of the combination of thoughts. נחת signifies here, as little as it does anywhere else, the rest of sloth; but rest, in contrast to such activity in labour as robs a man of himself, to the hunting after gain and honour which never has enough, to the rivalry which places its goal always higher and higher, and seeks to be before others - it is rest connected with well-being (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.5">Ecc 6:5</reference>), gentle quietness (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.17">Ecc 9:17</reference>), resting from self-activity (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.15">Isa 30:15</reference>); cf. the post-bibl. רוּח נחת, satisfaction, contentment, comfort. In a word, nahath has not here the sense of being idle or lazy. The sequence of the thoughts is this: The fool in idleness consumes his own life-strength; but, on the other hand, a little of true rest is better than the labour of windy effort, urged on by rivalry yielding no rest. כּף is the open hollow hand, and חפן (Assyr. ḥupunnu) the hand closed like a ball, the first. “Rest” and “labour and windy effort” are the accusatives of that to which the designation of measure refers (Gesen. §118. 3); the accus. connection lay here so much the nearer, as מלא is connected with the accus. of that with which anything is full. In “and windy effort” lies the reason for the judgment pronounced. The striving of a man who laboriously seeks only himself and loses himself in restlessness, is truly a striving which has wind for its object, and has the property of wind.
entries.3d01f791aa1eef3c77ce270f9f071b2711c07313: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.7-Eccl.4.8">Ecc 4:7-8</reference> “There is one without a second, also son and brother he has not; and there is no end of his labour; his eyes nevertheless are not satisfied with riches: For whom do I labour, then, and deny all good to my soul? Also this is vain, and it is a sore trouble.” That ואין, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.25">Psa 104:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.34">Psa 105:34</reference>, has the meaning of בּאין, <hi type="italic">absque</hi>, Nolde has already observed in his <hi type="italic">Partik.-Concordanz</hi>: a <hi type="italic">solitarius</hi>, without one standing by his side, a second standing near him, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, without wife and without friend; also, as the words following show, without son and brother. Regarding ואח, for which, with the connect. accus., ואח might be expected (cf. also <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.7">Ecc 2:7</reference>, וצאן with <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi>; and, on the other hand, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.23">Ecc 2:23</reference>, וכעס with <hi type="italic">Pashta</hi>), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Psa 55:10. <hi type="italic">Gam</hi> may be interpreted in the sense of “also” as well as of “nevertheless” (Ewald, 354a); the latter is to be preferred, since the endless labour includes in itself a restless striving after an increase of possession. The Kerî<, in an awkward way, changes עיניו into עינו; the taking together the two eyes as one would here be unnatural, since the avaricious man devours gold, silver, and precious things really with both his eyes, and yet, however great be his wealth, still more does he wish to see in his possession; the sing. of the pred. is as at <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.15">1Sa 4:15</reference>; Mic 4:11. <div eID="gen12266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12267" type="x-p"/> With <hi type="italic">ulmi ani</hi>, Koheleth puts himself in the place of such a friendless, childless man; yet this change of the description into a self-confession may be occasioned by this, that the author in his old age was really thus isolated, and stood alone. Regarding חסּר with the accus. of the person, to whom, and min of the matter, in respect of which there is want, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Psa 8:6. That the author stands in sympathy with the sorrowful condition here exposed, may also be remarked from the fact that he now proceeds to show the value of companionship and the miseries of isolation:
entries.76fed7c01f7f65cefbcc2e9cc1fd001a28781486: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.9">Ecc 4:9</reference> “Better are two together than one, seeing they have a good reward in their labour.” By hashshenaim, the author refers to such a pair; haehhad is one such as is just described. The good reward consists in this, that each one of the two has the pleasant consciousness of doing good to the other by his labour, and especially of being helpful to him. In this latter general sense is grounded the idea of the reward of faithful fellowship:
entries.1a6428d029b923401e23c97cb56adacd3bd04d10: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.10">Ecc 4:10</reference> “For if they fall, the one can raise up his fellow: but woe to the one who falleth, and there is not a second there to lift him up.” Only the Targ., which Grätz follows, confounds אילו<note placement="foot">With Munach and Rebia in one word, which, according to the masora, occurs in only four other places. <hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Mas. magna</hi> under this passage, and Mishpete hateamin 26 <hi type="italic">a</hi>.</note> with אילוּ; it is equivalent to אוי לו, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.9">Isa 3:9</reference>, or הוי לו, Eze 13:18. Haehhad is appos. connecting itself to the pronominal suff., as, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, in a far more inappropriate manner, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.2">Psa 86:2</reference>; the prep. is not in appos. usually repeated, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.19">Gen 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Gen 9:4</reference> (exceptions: Ps. 18:51; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.14">Psa 74:14</reference>). Whether we translate שׁיּפּל by <hi type="italic">qui ceciderit</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.3">Ecc 11:3</reference>), or by <hi type="italic">quum ceciderit</hi> (Jerome), is all one. יקים is potential: it is possible and probable that it will be done, provided he is a טוב חבר, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a true friend (<hi type="italic">Pirke aboth</hi>, ii. 13).
entries.e97db08c376a1ae9246c2bb61dd3fcd6f8cf4f31: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.11">Ecc 4:11</reference> “Moreover, if two lie together, then there is heat to them: but how can it be warm with one who is alone?” The marriage relation is not excluded, but it remains in the background; the author has two friends in his eye, who, lying in a cold night under one covering (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.26">Exo 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.20">Isa 28:20</reference>), cherish one another, and impart mutual warmth. Also in <hi type="italic">Aboth de-Rabbi Nathan</hi>, c. 8, the sleeping of two together is spoken of as an evidence of friendship. The <hi type="italic">vav</hi> in vehham is that of the consequent; it is wanting 10 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, according to rule, in haehhad, because it commonly comes into use with the verb, seldom (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.22.1">Gen 22:1</reference>) with the preceding subj.
entries.31d83ebe3c613a42542ce14f760e951668e5b19d: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.12">Ecc 4:12</reference> “And if one shall violently assail him who is alone, two shall withstand him; and (finally) a threefold cord is not quickly broken asunder.” The form yithqepho for yithqephehu, <reference osisRef="Job.15.24">Job 15:24</reference>, is like hirdepho, Hos 8:3 = hirdephehu, Jdg 9:40. If we take תקף in the sense of to overpower, then the meaning is: If one can overpower him who is alone, then, on the contrary, two can maintain their ground against him (Herzf.); but the two אם, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.10">Ecc 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.11">Ecc 4:11</reference>, which are equivalent to ἐάν, exclude such a pure logical εἰ. And why should תקף, if it can mean overpowering, not also mean doing violence to by means of a sudden attack? In the Mishnic and Arab. it signifies to seize, to lay hold of; in the Aram. אתקף = החזיק, and also at <reference osisRef="Job.14.20">Job 14:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.24">Job 15:24</reference> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Comm</hi>.), it may be understood of a violent assault, as well as of a completed subjugation; as נשׂא means to lift up and carry; עמד, to tread and to stand. But whether it be understood inchoat. or not, in any case האחד is not the assailant, who is much rather the unnamed subj. in יתקפי, but the one (the <hi type="italic">solitarius</hi>) who, if he is alone, must succumb; the construction of hithqepho haehhad follows the scheme of <reference osisRef="Exod.2.6">Exo 2:6</reference>, “she saw it, the child.” To the assault expressed by תקף, there stands opposed the expression נגד עמד, which means to withstand any one with success; as עמד לפני, 2Ki 10:4; <reference osisRef="Ps.147.17">Psa 147:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.7">Dan 8:7</reference>, means to maintain one’s ground. Of three who hold together, 12 <hi type="italic">a</hi> says nothing; the advance from two to three is thus made in the manner of a numerical proverb (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Proverbs</hi>, vol. I p. 13). If two hold together, that is seen to be good; but if there be three, this threefold bond is likened to a cord formed of three threads, which cannot easily be broken. Instead of the definite specific art. הח הם, we make use of the indefinite. <hi type="italic">Funiculus triplex difficile rumpitur</hi> is one of the winged expressions used by Koheleth.
entries.164bb1d1ff5fb23900c18c918a45261b3c80e285: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.13">Ecc 4:13</reference> “Better is a youth poor and wise, than a king old and foolish, who no longer understands how to be warned,” - <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, who increases his folly by this, that he is “wise in his own eyes,” <reference osisRef="Prov.26.12">Pro 26:12</reference>; earlier, as עוד denotes, he was, in some measure, accessible to the instruction of others in respect of what was wanting to him; but now in his advanced age he is hardened in his folly, bids defiance to all warning counsel, and undermines his throne. The connection of the verb ידע with ל and the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. (for which elsewhere only the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. is used) is a favourite form with the author; it means to know anything well, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.1">Ecc 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.8">Ecc 6:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.15">Ecc 10:15</reference>; here is meant an understanding resting on the knowledge of oneself and on the knowledge of men. נזהר is here and at <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.12">Ecc 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.12">Psa 19:12</reference>, a <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. <hi type="italic">tolerativum</hi>, such as the synon. נוסר, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.10">Psa 2:10</reference> : to let oneself be cleared up, made wiser, enlightened, warned. After this contrast, the idea connected with חכם also defines itself. A young man (ילד, as at <reference osisRef="Dan.1.4">Dan 1:4</reference>, but also <reference osisRef="Gen.4.23">Gen 4:23</reference>) is meant who (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., above, p. 639, under misken) yet excels the old imbecile and childish king, in that he perceives the necessity of a fundamental change in the present state of public matters, and knows how to master the situation to such a degree that he raises himself to the place of ruler over the neglected community.
entries.2837b592a63f93b524a26b6dbcf5c40d916e53e4: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.14">Ecc 4:14</reference> “For out of the prison-house he goeth forth to reign as king, although he was born as a poor man in his kingdom.” With כּי the properties of poverty and wisdom attributed to the young man are verified, - wisdom in this, that he knew how to find the way from a prison to a throne. As harammim, <reference osisRef="2Chr.22.5">2Ch 22:5</reference> = haarammim, 2Ki 8:28, so hasurim = haasurim (cf. masoreth = maasoreth, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.37">Eze 20:37</reference>); beth haasirim (Kerı̂; haasurim), Jdg 16:21, Jdg 16:25, and beth haesur, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.15">Jer 38:15</reference>, designate the prison; cf. <hi type="italic">Moëd katan</hi>, Ecc 3:1. The modern form of the language prefers this elision of the א, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, אפלּוּ = אף אלּוּ, אלתּר = אל־אתר, בּתר <hi type="italic">post</hi> = בּאתר <hi type="italic">contra</hi>, etc. The perf. יחא is also thought of as having reached the throne, and having pre-eminence assigned to him as such. He has come forth from the prison to become king, רשׁ ... כּי. Zöckler translates: “Whereas also he that was born in his kingdom was poor,” and adds the remark: “גם כי, after the כי of the preceding clause, does not so much introduce a verification of it, as much rather an intensification; by which is expressed, that the prisoner has not merely transitorily fallen into such misery, but that he was born in poor and lowly circumstances, and that in his own kingdom בּם, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, in the same land which he should afterwards rule as king.” But גם כי is nowhere used by Koheleth in the sense of “<hi type="italic">ja auch</hi>” (= whereas also); and also where it is thus to be translated, as at <reference osisRef="Jer.14.18">Jer 14:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.11">Jer 23:11</reference>, it is used in the sense of “<hi type="italic">denn auch</hi>” (= for also), assigning proof. The fact is, that this group of particles, according as כי is thought of as demonst. or relat., means either “<hi type="italic">denn auch</hi>,” <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.16">Ecc 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.22">Ecc 7:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.16">Ecc 8:16</reference>, or “<hi type="italic">wenn auch</hi>” = ἐὰν καί, as here and at Ecc 8:12. In the latter case, it is related to כּי גּם (sometimes also merely גּם, <reference osisRef="Ps.95.9">Psa 95:9</reference>; Mal 3:15), as ἐὰν (εἰ) καί, although, notwithstanding, is to καὶ ἐάν (εἰ), even although.<note placement="foot">That the accentuation separates the two words גם־ כי is to be judged from this, that it almost everywhere prefers אם־ כי (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <hi type="italic">Comm</hi>. to <reference osisRef="Ps.1.2">Psa 1:2</reference>).</note> <div eID="gen12267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12268" type="x-p"/> Thus 14 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, connecting itself with למלך, is to be translated: “although he was born (נולד,not נולד) in his kingdom as a poor man.”<note placement="foot">נולד רש cannot mean “to become poor.” Grätz appeals to the Mishnic language; but no intelligent linguist will use נולד רשׁ of a man in any other sense than that he is originally poor.</note> <div eID="gen12268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12269" type="x-p"/> We cannot also concur with Zöckler in the view that the suff. of : b refers to the young upstart: in the kingdom which should afterwards become his; for this reason, that the suff. of תח, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.4.16">Ecc 4:16</reference></hi>, refers to the old king, and thus also that this designation may be mediated, בם must refer to him. מלכות signifies kingdom, reign, realm; here, the realm, as at <reference osisRef="Neh.9.35">Neh 9:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.11">Dan 5:11</reference>; 6:29. Grätz thinks <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.13-Eccl.4.16">Ecc 4:13-16</reference> ought to drive expositors to despair. But hitherto we have found no room for despair in obtaining a meaning from them. What follows also does not perplex us. The author describes how all the world hails the entrance of the new youthful king on his government, and gathers together under his sceptre.
entries.ee3e981dc79494e8486e77f3ab849dfd06a913e7: <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.15-Eccl.4.16">Ecc 4:15-16</reference> “I saw all the living which walk under the sun on the side of the youth, the second who shall enter upon the place of the former: no end of all the people, all those at whose head he stands.” The author, by the expression “I saw,” places himself back in the time of the change of government. If we suppose that he represents this to himself in a lively manner, then the words are to be translated: of the second who shall be his successor; but if we suppose that he seeks to express from the standpoint of the past that which, lying farther back in the past, was now for the first time future, then the future represents the time to come in the past, as at 2Ki 3:27; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.6">Psa 78:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.28">Job 15:28</reference> (Hitz.): of the second who should enter on his place (עמד, to step to, to step forth, of the new king, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.23">Dan 8:23</reference>; Dan 11:2.; cf. קוּם, 1Ki 8:20). The designation of the crowd which, as the pregnant עם expresses, gathered by the side of the young successor to the old king, by “all the living, those walking under the sun (המה, perhaps intentionally the pathetic word for הלכים, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.5">Isa 42; 5</reference>),),” would remain a hyperbole, even although the throne of the Asiatic world-ruler had been intended; still the expression, so absolute in its universality, would in that case be more natural (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the conjectural reference to Cyrus and Astygates). השּׁני, Ewald refers to the successor to the king, the second after the king, and translates: “to the second man who should reign in his stead;” but the second man in this sense has certainly never been the child of fortune; one must then think of Joseph, who, however, remains the second man. Hitzig rightly: “The youth is the second שׁני, not אחר, in contrast to the king, who, as his predecessor, is the first.” “Yet,” he continues, “הילד should be the appos. and השׁני the principal word,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, instead of: with the second youth, was to be expected: with the second, the youth. It is true, we may either translate: with the second youth, or: with the second, the youth - the  form of expression has in its something incorrect, for it has the appearance as if it treated of two youths.
